title: Sergius of Radonezh
hook: a Russian hermit in the forest who shared bread with a bear and founded a great monastery

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregory Palamas and the monks of Athos, praying in stillness for the light that shone on the mountain. Your line was the light of tabor. Where did a little light find you in the dark? Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

One piece of bread, sitting on a tree stump at the edge of a clearing. That's the whole scene. Deep in a Russian forest, a young man has built himself a small wooden cell and a chapel with his own hands. No village nearby. No road worth the name. And one day, the old account says, a bear comes out of the trees, hungry, and stands looking at him. He doesn't run. He goes inside, brings out a piece of his bread, and sets it on the stump. The bear eats it and goes away. And then it comes back. Again and again. Today: Sergius of Radonezh.
screen: `ONE PIECE OF BREAD ON A STUMP.`
`A BEAR COMES OUT OF THE TREES.`

segments.voice: Sergius is a monk the Russian Orthodox Church honors as a saint, and his story comes down to us through a Life written by a monk named Epiphanius. As a young man, the Life says, Sergius went into the forest to live alone with God. He chopped his own wood and grew what he could. He prayed. And the bear kept coming. Here's the detail the Life lingers on. Some days Sergius had only one piece of bread. And on those days, the story goes, he gave it to the bear and went hungry himself, rather than send the animal away with nothing. That's an odd kind of holiness. Not a sermon. A crust, and a stomach left empty. Other Christian stories, too, put holy people at peace with wild animals, and the Gospel of Mark has a small line about Jesus in the desert, in the King James Bible: "and was with the wild beasts". The wilderness isn't only danger in these stories. It's also a place where creatures and a person at prayer learn to live side by side. Sergius didn't stay alone. Other monks heard about him and came to the forest to live near him. Cells went up around his. A community grew, and it was dedicated to the Holy Trinity. The Life remembers him as a leader who still carried water, baked bread and wore patched clothes. A monastery grew where his cell had been. But the scene that stays is smaller: the stump, and the bread, and the bear.

Here's the practice: share with a creature. Take a moment to think of an animal near your life. A pet on the couch. The birds outside. A neighbor's dog. A squirrel that raids the feeder. What could you set out for it today? Fresh water. A few seeds. A walk, or simply your patience. Choose one small thing. Then sit with that creature in mind, the way Sergius sat at the edge of his clearing. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, just let it be in your thoughts, as it is. The bell holds the time.
Sergius. A forest hermit of Radonezh honored by the Orthodox Church, who shared his bread with a bear and around whom a community of the Holy Trinity grew.
Your line: bread with the bear. Today, when something hungry comes to your door, a creature or a person, give from what you actually have, even if it's the last piece. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: The Russian Orthodox Church honors Sergius of Radonezh as a saint, and the Trinity monastery that grew up around his forest cell bears his name; his story with the bear is told in his Life.

options: eat it yourself; the bear can find its own food.
give the bear your last piece and go hungry.
bar the door and wait for it to leave.
fork.reveal: the Life says that on days like that, Sergius gave the bear his bread and went without.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cute story about a monk and a bear.
what it means: a hermit who gave away his last bread rather than turn a hungry creature away, and a community that grew around that kind of life.
what a scholar hears: the Life of Sergius by his disciple Epiphanius, and an old Christian theme of holy people living peaceably with wild beasts in the wilderness.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or counts used. The bear episode, the last-piece detail, the arrival of other monks, the Trinity dedication and his manual work are taken from Epiphanius's Life (as revised by Pachomius); confirm each is in the Life.
'Epiphanius, who lived with his disciples': Epiphanius the Wise is usually described as a monk of the Trinity monastery and a disciple of Sergius; confirm phrasing.
'Orthodox Christians in Russia still travel to the monastery that bears his name' (the Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius) is general knowledge, not from a cited text; confirm or trim.
